entry:
I keep thinking about how this started: not with a missing feature, but with broken trust. The ledger could move, but you couldn't lean on it. These three passes were really three layers of trust-building.

The first pass was identity and truth at rest. Making event_id NOT NULL UNIQUE and moving ULID generation server-side felt like putting a spine into the system. Backfill and quarantine were the hard-earned admission that history is messy, and integrity means facing that mess directly instead of pretending it isn't there.

The second pass was continuity in motion. Embedding the reconciler and stamping replication timestamps on the server turned replication from "best effort" into accountable behavior. The system now tells the truth about when it knew what, and that matters more than speed when correctness is the product.

The third pass was operational humility: leases, jitter, backoff, caps, degraded mode, atomic stamp. That's the part that says, "we don't trust happy paths; we trust guardrails." It was less glamorous, but it made the whole thing survivable under pressure.

What drove me through three back-to-back passes was the feeling that half-fixes are a tax on everyone who comes after. I wanted the next engineer to inherit a system that fails predictably, recovers intentionally, and doesn't gaslight you at 2 a.m.

From the engineer's chair, "operational" doesn't feel like celebration first. It feels like exhale. Like the dashboard stopped arguing with reality. Like you can finally distinguish normal variance from actual danger. It's not perfect, but it is honest now—and honest systems are the only ones you can responsibly scale.
